choices.text: A mixture of the sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids
A mixture of triacylglycerols from animal fat
choices.why: Triacylglycerols are the starting fats. Soap is made from them by hydrolysis with alkali.

choices.text: A mixture of salts of long-chain alkylbenzenesulfonic acids
choices.why: Those are synthetic detergents, which were developed to avoid the hard-water problem of soaps.

choices.text: A mixture of glycerol and excess alkali
choices.why: Glycerol and excess alkali are impurities in crude soap curds; they are removed when soap is purified.

explanation: Soap is a mixture of the sodium or potassium salts of the long-chain fatty acids produced by hydrolysis (saponification) of animal fat with alkali.

prompt: When one molecule of a fat (a triacylglycerol) is saponified with sodium hydroxide and water, how many molecules of sodium carboxylate (soap) form along with one glycerol?
explanation: A fat is a triester of glycerol, so saponification with NaOH breaks all three ester bonds, giving glycerol and three sodium carboxylate (soap) molecules.

prompt: What are the products of saponifying glyceryl dioleate monopalmitate with aqueous NaOH?

choices.text: Glycerol, 2 sodium oleate, and 1 sodium palmitate
Glycerol, 1 sodium oleate, and 2 sodium palmitate
choices.why: The name says dioleate (two oleate groups) and monopalmitate (one palmitate group), so the counts are reversed here.

choices.text: Glycerol, 2 oleic acid, and 1 sodium palmitate
choices.why: In aqueous NaOH all three acids come off as sodium salts, not one as the free acid.

choices.text: Sodium glycerate, oleic acid, and palmitic acid
choices.why: Saponification gives glycerol itself, and the fatty acids leave as their sodium salts.

explanation: Exercise 27.2.2: glyceryl dioleate monopalmitate → glycerol + 2 sodium oleate + sodium palmitate. Each ester bond is hydrolyzed, and in aqueous NaOH each fatty acid ends up as its sodium carboxylate.

prompt: How are crude soap curds purified?

choices.text: By boiling with water and adding NaCl or KCl to precipitate the pure carboxylate salts
By adding more NaOH to dissolve the glycerol
choices.why: Crude curds already contain excess alkali. Purification uses NaCl or KCl to precipitate the carboxylate salts.

choices.text: By adding magnesium and calcium salts to precipitate the soap
choices.why: Magnesium and calcium carboxylates are the insoluble scum that forms in hard water, not purified soap.

choices.text: By catalytic hydrogenation over nickel
choices.why: Hydrogenation reduces C=C bonds in oils (Section 27.1); it doesn't remove glycerol and alkali from soap.

explanation: Crude soap curds contain glycerol and excess alkali as well as soap. Boiling with water and adding NaCl or KCl precipitates the pure carboxylate salts, which are dried, perfumed, and pressed into bars.

prompt: Why can soaps act as cleansers?

choices.text: Each molecule has an ionic, hydrophilic carboxylate end and a nonpolar, hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail
Each molecule is nonpolar throughout, so it dissolves grease directly
choices.why: The carboxylate end is ionic and attracted to water. A soap works because its two ends behave so differently.

choices.text: Each molecule is ionic throughout, so it is strongly attracted to water only
choices.why: The long hydrocarbon tail is nonpolar and hydrophobic, which is what lets soap attract oils.

choices.text: The hydrocarbon tail is hydrophilic and the carboxylate end is hydrophobic
choices.why: It's the reverse: the ionic carboxylate end is hydrophilic and the hydrocarbon tail is hydrophobic.

explanation: The carboxylate end of a soap molecule is ionic and therefore hydrophilic. The long hydrocarbon portion is nonpolar and hydrophobic, more soluble in oils. Because soaps are attracted to both oils and water, they are useful as cleansers.

prompt: When soap is dispersed in water and forms micelles, how are the molecules arranged?

choices.text: Hydrocarbon tails cluster inside, and ionic heads on the surface protrude into the water
Ionic heads cluster inside, and hydrocarbon tails protrude into the water
choices.why: That is backward. The hydrophobic tails avoid water and gather in the center.

choices.text: The molecules line up in a flat double layer with heads on both faces
choices.why: That describes the lipid bilayer that phospholipids form (Section 27.3). Soap micelles are spherical clusters.

choices.text: Tails and heads are mixed randomly throughout a spherical cluster
choices.why: The arrangement isn't random: tails form a tangled hydrophobic ball and heads cover the surface.

explanation: In water, the long hydrocarbon tails cluster on the inside of a tangled, hydrophobic ball while the ionic heads on the surface protrude into the water. These spherical clusters are called micelles (Figure 27.2.1).

prompt: How does soap let grease be rinsed away with water?

choices.text: Grease droplets are coated by the hydrophobic tails in the center of micelles and so are solubilized in water
The carboxylate heads react with the grease to form water-soluble esters
choices.why: No reaction occurs. The grease is carried in the hydrophobic center of the micelles.

choices.text: The soap hydrolyzes the grease into glycerol and fatty acids
choices.why: Cleansing is a physical process: micelles take up the grease, they don't hydrolyze it.

choices.text: The ionic heads surround the grease while the tails point into the water
choices.why: The grease is nonpolar, so it is coated by the nonpolar tails; the ionic heads face the water.

explanation: Grease and oil droplets are solubilized in water when they are coated by the nonpolar, hydrophobic tails of soap molecules in the center of micelles. Once solubilized, the grease and dirt can be rinsed away.

prompt: What goes wrong when soap is used in hard water?

choices.text: The soluble sodium carboxylates are converted into insoluble magnesium and calcium salts, leaving scum
The soap is hydrogenated by metal ions and becomes a solid fat
choices.why: Metal ions don't hydrogenate anything. They form insoluble carboxylate salts with the soap.

choices.text: The soap is converted back into a triacylglycerol
choices.why: Hard water doesn't re-form fats. The magnesium and calcium ions it contains precipitate the carboxylates.

choices.text: The sodium carboxylates become insoluble sodium salts of sulfonic acids
choices.why: Sulfonates are the synthetic detergents chemists made to avoid this problem; they aren't formed in hard water.

explanation: Hard water contains metal ions. Soluble sodium carboxylates are converted into insoluble magnesium and calcium salts, leaving the ring of scum around bathtubs and a gray tinge on white clothes.

prompt: Magnesium oleate, a component of bathtub scum, contains Mg^2+ and oleate ions, CH3(CH2)7CH=CH(CH2)7CO2^−. How many oleate ions are there for each Mg^2+ ion?
explanation: Each oleate carboxylate carries a 1− charge and magnesium carries 2+, so two oleate ions balance one Mg^2+: [CH3(CH2)7CH=CH(CH2)7CO2^−]2 Mg^2+ (Exercise 27.2.1).

prompt: How do synthetic alkylbenzenesulfonate detergents differ from soaps?

choices.text: They don't form insoluble metal salts in hard water, so they leave no scum
They clean by a completely different mechanism that doesn't involve a nonpolar end
choices.why: The mechanism is the same as for soaps: the alkylbenzene end is attracted to grease and the anionic sulfonate end to water.

choices.text: Their ionic end is a carboxylate rather than a sulfonate
choices.why: Soaps have the carboxylate end; detergents have an anionic sulfonate end.

choices.text: They are made by saponification of animal fat with alkali
choices.why: That is how soap is made. Detergents are synthesized as salts of long-chain alkylbenzenesulfonic acids.

explanation: Synthetic detergents are salts of long-chain alkylbenzenesulfonic acids. They work the same way as soaps, but unlike soaps they don't form insoluble metal salts in hard water and don't leave an unpleasant scum.
